landmark_cases.title: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife
landmark_cases.reason: Canonical articulation of Article III standing’s three elements—injury in fact, causation, and redressability—and the requirement that injury be concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent.

landmark_cases.title: Summers v. Earth Island Institute
landmark_cases.reason: Establishes that a bare procedural right, without a concrete harm to a plaintiff’s own interests, does not confer standing—central to rejecting procedural-rights-in-vacuo theories.

landmark_cases.title: FEC v. Akins
landmark_cases.reason: Defines informational standing: a concrete injury exists when a plaintiff is denied information that a statute entitles the plaintiff to receive; frames the analysis of claimed informational harms.

landmark_cases.title: Heckler v. Chaney
landmark_cases.reason: Seminal rule that agency nonenforcement decisions are generally unreviewable, informing the causation/redressability analysis where relief depends on discretionary enforcement choices.

landmark_cases.title: Food and Drug Administration v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine
landmark_cases.reason: Reaffirms that standing cannot rest on speculation about the independent decisions of third parties not before the court—key to the causation and redressability analysis here.

landmark_cases.title: Florida Audubon Society v. Bentsen
landmark_cases.reason: D.C. Circuit en banc precedent on procedural-injury standing: explains the limited relaxation of imminence and redressability, while still requiring a concrete, particularized injury.
